screens.title: What is plane detection?
screens.narratorSegment: Plane detection is the process where the AR platform analyzes camera images and device motion to identify flat, roughly planar surfaces in the environment. A detected plane is represented as a trackable with a pose — a position and rotation in 3D space — and a boundary polygon that outlines the shape and size of the area recognized so far. This gives your app three essential pieces of information: where to place objects, how to orient them to match the surface, and the usable area so you avoid placing content beyond the detected region. For example, if a table is detected, the AR system reports the table's center pose and a polygon that follows its visible edges; you can then place a model so it sits flush with the table top. A common misconception is to expect a perfectly complete polygon immediately. In reality, plane polygons refine over time as the system receives more visual data: they can grow, shrink, and merge. That means your placement logic should tolerate updates — avoid relying on a single momentary polygon size. Key takeaway: treat detected planes as evolving anchors that provide pose and boundary information you can use for grounded placement, but always handle updates and merges gracefully.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A plane trackable provides a pose and boundary polygon. It evolves as the AR system refines its understanding.

content.html:
Core Concept

Plane detection

A trackable surface with a pose and a polygonal boundary that refines over time.

Pose
Position and rotation where objects can be anchored.
Boundary polygon
A polygon that defines the currently detected extents of the plane.
Updates
Planes can grow, shrink, or merge as the AR system refines its map.
Key Takeaway

Treat planes as evolving anchors. Use pose for placement and boundary polygon to limit where you spawn objects.

Analogy — think of plane detection like mapping a table with a flashlight
At first you only see a corner. As you move the light, you see more edges and the shape grows. The AR system behaves the same as it gains more visual data.
Concrete Example
If the AR SDK reports a plane pose at position X and a polygon that approximates a small rectangle, instantiate a coffee cup model at that pose so its base aligns with the plane. Continue monitoring plane updates — if the polygon later expands, your cup remains anchored to the pose but you can enable additional interactions to relocate it if needed.
Common mistake
Expecting an instant perfect polygon; noisy or textureless surfaces may delay detection.
Pro tip
Allow the UI to indicate scanning progress and avoid forced early placement until a plane stabilizes.

screens.title: AR Plane Manager and AR Plane objects
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's AR Foundation provides the AR Plane Manager to bridge the underlying AR SDK's plane detections into your scene. When you add an AR Plane Manager to the AR Session Origin, it listens for plane trackable events and can instantiate a prefab to represent each detected plane. That prefab should include a Mesh Renderer/Mesh Filter or a simple Quad and an AR Plane component so the manager recognizes it as a visual representation. The AR Plane Manager can be configured to detect horizontal, vertical, or both plane types; choose the types your experience requires to reduce noise. As the AR system updates planes, the AR Plane Manager updates the corresponding GameObjects so the pose and mesh reflect the refined polygon. A common misunderstanding is thinking the manager itself performs detection; instead, it coordinates detections from ARCore/ARKit and manages Unity GameObjects. Practical example: create a semi‑transparent quad prefab named ARPlaneVisualizer, assign a translucent material, add the AR Plane component, and drag that prefab into the Plane Prefab slot on the AR Plane Manager. This ensures visible feedback during testing and helps users and developers see what the runtime perceives as usable surface. Close by asking: how will you tune plane types and materials to balance visibility and real‑world readability?

keyIdea.title: How it works
keyIdea.text: AR Plane Manager converts platform plane data into Unity GameObjects using a prefab that contains an AR Plane component and a visible mesh.

content.html:
Definition

AR Plane Manager

A manager that receives platform plane detections and instantiates Unity representations using your prefab.

Detect types
Configure horizontal, vertical, or both to suit your scene and reduce false positives.
Prefab requirement
Prefab should include a mesh and an AR Plane component so the manager can attach data and update mesh boundaries.
Dynamic updates
As the system refines planes, the AR Plane Manager updates pose and mesh geometry automatically.
Visualization example
Create a quad prefab, assign a translucent material (fade or transparent), attach an AR Plane component, and set this prefab in the Plane Prefab slot of AR Plane Manager.
Scenario
You're testing on a wooden table: enabling horizontal detection and a light blue translucent prefab makes the table's area obvious while still showing texture underneath for context. If you only need walls, disable horizontal detection to save processing and reduce clutter.
Mistake
Leaving the Plane Prefab empty makes planes invisible even though tracking may be working.
Takeaway
Always provide a visible prefab and test in varied lighting to validate detection behavior.

screens.title: Creating a plane visualization prefab
screens.narratorSegment: Making a clear plane visual is a small authoring step that pays off during testing and user interaction. The process begins in Unity's Project window: create a Quad or simple mesh and name it 'ARPlaneVisualizer'. Next, create a material and choose a translucent rendering mode such as Fade or Transparent; pick a light, distinctive tint so planes are visible without obscuring the camera feed. Assign that material to the quad so the real world remains visible beneath the visual. Add the AR Plane component to the visual so Unity treats the prefab properly when instantiated by AR Plane Manager. Finally, convert the GameObject into a prefab by dragging it into Assets and then delete the scene instance to keep the hierarchy clean. A common mistake is using an opaque material — doing so hides real-world cues and confuses testing. Practical example: use a pale blue with alpha around 40% so the boundary is easy to see while still revealing floor or tabletop texture. When done, assign this prefab to the Plane Prefab slot on the AR Plane Manager attached to your AR Session Origin. Practice this sequence to make plane detection immediately visible on device builds.

keyIdea.title: Prefab steps
keyIdea.text: Create a quad, set a translucent material, add AR Plane component, make into a prefab, and assign to AR Plane Manager.

content.html:
Process Flow

Create AR Plane Visualizer

  1. Create Quad: In Project, Create → 3D Object → Quad. Name it ARPlaneVisualizer.
  2. Create Material: New Material, set to URP Lit or Standard, choose Fade/Transparent rendering, set alpha ~40%.
  3. Assign Material: Drag material onto Quad so plane is translucent and colored.
  4. Add AR Plane: Add an AR Plane component to the visual so the manager recognizes it.
  5. Make Prefab: Drag the GameObject into Assets and delete the scene copy.
Why translucency matters

A translucent plane makes it obvious where the AR system perceives the surface while still allowing the user to see the real texture. This avoids confusion during testing and improves spatial context for users placing objects.

Example values
Albedo: light blue. Rendering Mode: Fade. Alpha: 100–150 on 0–255 scale (around 40%). These settings keep the plane visible without blocking the camera feed.
Key Takeaway

A simple translucent prefab makes detection visible. Never ship opaque plane visuals to avoid hiding the real view.

screens.title: Placing an object with ARRaycastManager
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the core placement logic that turns a screen touch into a world pose and a spawned object. The ARRaycastManager handles raycasts against trackables such as detected planes. In the provided script, the script gets the ARRaycastManager reference in Awake, then in Update checks for touches. When a touch begins, the code calls Raycast with TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon so hits are restricted to the interior of detected plane polygons. If a hit exists, it uses the first hit's pose to instantiate the prefab at that position with the plane's rotation. A concrete example: tapping the tabletop sends a ray through the camera frustum that intersects the plane polygon where the table was detected; the script instantiates the cube prefab at that pose so it visually rests on the table. A common misconception is assuming raycasts return every frame without touches; raycasts should be targeted on user input to avoid unnecessary instantiation. Also, because planes update, instantiated objects reference the pose at spawn time — consider parenting objects or reanchoring them if you need them to follow a plane's geometry later. This script is intentionally small so you can extend it to check for multiple hits, add placement indicators, or constrain placement by plane size.

keyIdea.title: Placement logic
keyIdea.text: Use ARRaycastManager.Raycast with PlaneWithinPolygon on touch to get a Pose, then Instantiate the prefab at that pose.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

ARPlacementManager.cs (core excerpt)

using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class ARPlacementManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  [SerializeField]
  private GameObject objectToPlace;

  private ARRaycastManager arRaycastManager;
  private static List<ARRaycastHit> hits = new List<ARRaycastHit>();

  void Awake()
  {
    arRaycastManager = GetComponent<ARRaycastManager>();
  }

  void Update()
  {
    if (Input.touchCount > 0)
    {
      Touch touch = Input.GetTouch(0);

      if (touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began)
      {
        if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
        {
          Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;
          Instantiate(objectToPlace, hitPose.position, hitPose.rotation);
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
This small script demonstrates essential placement: get the ARRaycastManager, raycast on touch, and instantiate the object at the returned pose.
Step-by-step explanation
  • Awake: cache ARRaycastManager so raycasts are available.
  • Input: check touch count and phase to act only on initial press.
  • Raycast: use PlaneWithinPolygon to get valid hits inside plane boundaries.
  • Instantiate: use hitPose.position and .rotation to spawn the object aligned with the plane.
Misconception
Assuming TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon will return hits outside the polygon; it will not. Use other trackable types for different behaviours.
Key Takeaway

Raycasts convert user input into precise world poses. Use the returned pose to instantiate objects so they appear anchored to detected planes.

screens.title: AR Session and AR Session Origin
screens.narratorSegment: Two foundational GameObjects control the AR runtime in Unity: AR Session and AR Session Origin. AR Session manages the lifecycle — starting, pausing, and stopping tracking — and acts as the bridge to the platform's tracking engine. AR Session Origin is the coordinate translation layer: it maps the real‑world tracking coordinate system provided by ARKit or ARCore into Unity's world space so your virtual content appears in the correct physical location. The AR Camera is commonly a child of AR Session Origin; when the device moves, the AR Camera's transform changes to keep the background and overlays aligned. A common pitfall is adding AR Plane Manager or ARRaycastManager to a GameObject outside AR Session Origin; both should be on AR Session Origin or a child so their trackable coordinates match the origin's coordinate space. For example, if you spawn content under AR Session Origin, and then later accidentally move the origin, all your virtual content will shift relative to the camera. Key practical check: when things drift or placement seems offset, inspect whether AR Session Origin has been scaled, rotated, or otherwise modified. The main takeaway is that AR Session handles tracking lifecycle while AR Session Origin defines where and how trackables map into your Unity scene.

keyIdea.title: Session vs Origin
keyIdea.text: AR Session manages tracking lifecycle. AR Session Origin maps the platform coordinate system into Unity so virtual objects align with the real world.

content.html:
Architecture

AR Session & AR Session Origin

These components work together so tracking data aligns correctly with Unity objects and camera rendering.
AR Session
Manages the AR lifecycle and interfaces with the underlying platform for tracking state.
AR Session Origin
Translates platform coordinates into Unity's world space; AR components should live on it or its children.
AR Camera
Usually a child of AR Session Origin and renders the camera feed with overlays for virtual objects.
Practical checks
  • Ensure AR Plane Manager and ARRaycastManager are on AR Session Origin or its child to keep trackable coordinates consistent.
  • Avoid transforming AR Session Origin manually after tracking starts; unexpected translations or rotations lead to misalignment.
  • If objects drift, check tracking quality and whether AR Session has been paused or restarted during runtime.
Scenario
If a placed object appears offset when you walk around, examine whether the AR Session Origin was moved or scaled at author time, or whether the AR Camera is not correctly parented.
Key Takeaway

Keep AR managers on AR Session Origin. Treat the origin as your reference frame to avoid placement and tracking errors.

screens.title: Plane lifecycle and updates
screens.narratorSegment: Detected planes have a lifecycle: they are created when enough features are found, updated as new observations expand or refine their boundary, merged when overlapping detections represent the same surface, and sometimes removed when tracking loses confidence. Understanding this lifecycle helps you build robust placement and UI behaviors. For example, when two small plane polygons merge into one larger polygon, an object you previously anchored to the first plane still has its original pose; the AR Plane Manager will update mesh geometry but not necessarily reparent or reposition your object — your code should decide if it needs to re-anchor or keep the original pose. A concrete example: you detect two adjacent patches on a long table; as you walk, the SDK merges them into a single plane. If your placement logic expects a fixed polygon size, placements near the seam could be rejected earlier and accepted later. A common mistake is assuming plane boundaries are permanent. Instead, design UI affordances that indicate scanning is ongoing and either delay final placement until a plane stabilizes or allow users to move objects after placement. The key insight is planning for dynamic updates — handle creates, updates, merges, and removals gracefully so content remains believable and stable.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Planes are dynamic: create → update → merge → remove. Design placement logic to tolerate polygon and pose changes.

content.html:
Process Flow

Plane lifecycle

Create: AR SDK reports a new trackable when features cohere. Update: boundary polygon and pose refine. Merge: overlapping planes combine into single trackable. Remove: low confidence or out‑of‑view planes may be discarded.
Create
When initial features indicate a flat surface.
Update
Polygon grows or refines with more observations.
Merge
Two trackables representing the same surface combine into one.
Remove
Planes may be removed if tracking confidence drops.
Key Takeaway

Expect plane geometry to change. Allow your app to reanchor, relocate, or allow user adjustments rather than assume fixed boundaries.

Concrete scenario
You place a vase near the edge between two detected patches. Later the engine merges those patches into a single larger plane. If your app depended on the earlier small polygon for placement validation, it might need to update the object's allowed interactions after the merge.
Design suggestion
Provide a brief scanning state UI and allow users to confirm placement or to move objects after initial placement. This reduces surprises when planes change.

screens.title: Raycast types and placement choices
screens.narratorSegment: ARRaycastManager supports different TrackableType flags that control what surfaces raycasts can hit. TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon confines hits to the interior of a detected plane's boundary — a good default for placing objects strictly on a known surface. If you need hits on estimated infinite planes or approximate ground alignment, other flags or custom logic may be appropriate. For example, PlaneWithinPolygon prevents placement on the invisible extension of a table beyond the detected area, which is often what you want to avoid floating objects or unexpected overlaps. A contrasting choice is using PlaneEstimated or FeaturePoint hits when you want looser placement semantics: feature points let you place on textured surfaces that were not yet consolidated into a plane, but they are less stable. A common mistake is mixing trackable types without understanding stability tradeoffs; using feature points can yield placements that look correct momentarily but drift as tracking refines. Concrete example: for a furniture placement app, use PlaneWithinPolygon for reliable anchored placement on tabletops and floors. For an exploratory game that places ephemeral items in rough locations, feature or estimated hits may be acceptable. The core decision is balancing placement stability against availability when surfaces are difficult to detect.

A contrasting choice is using PlaneEstimated or FeaturePoint hits when you want looser placement semantics: feature points let you place on textured surfaces that were not yet consolidated into a plane, but they are less stable. A common mistake is mixing trackable types without understanding stability tradeoffs; using feature points can yield placements that look correct momentarily but drift as tracking refines. Concrete example: for a furniture placement app, use PlaneWithinPolygon for reliable anchored placement on tabletops and floors. For an exploratory game that places ephemeral items in rough locations, feature or estimated hits may be acceptable. The core decision is balancing placement stability against availability when surfaces are difficult to detect.

content.html:
Comparison

Trackable types for raycasts

PlaneWithinPolygon
Hits only inside detected plane boundaries. Best for precise anchored placement.
PlaneEstimated
Returns an estimated plane even if full polygon isn't available. Useful when immediate placement is required but less precise.
FeaturePoints
Hits on detected feature points allow placement in textured but non‑planar regions; stability varies.
Decision guide
  • Use PlaneWithinPolygon for furniture, product previews, or anything needing a firm anchor.
  • Use estimated or feature hits only when immediate availability is more important than long-term stability.
  • Test placements in low‑texture and reflective environments to validate chosen trackable types.
Example
A floor‑placing app uses PlaneWithinPolygon for stable furniture placement. An art app that spawns ephemeral particles may use feature points for playful placement even if they jitter slightly later.
Key Takeaway

Match raycast types to your UX: prefer stability for anchored content and looser types when availability or immediacy is more important.

screens.title: Common issues and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When plane visuals don't appear or placed objects drift, a few recurring causes explain most situations. First, if plane visuals are missing, check whether the Plane Prefab slot on AR Plane Manager is empty or the assigned prefab lacks an AR Plane component. Without that prefab, the manager has nothing to instantiate visually even though detection may be happening. Second, poor tracking due to textureless surfaces, low light, or reflective materials reduces feature points and delays plane creation. A practical diagnostic is to move the device slowly across textured regions; if detection improves, tracking conditions were the culprit. Third, if objects drift, confirm AR Session Origin and AR Camera are set up correctly and not being transformed after tracking begins. Also check that the AR Session hasn't been restarted unexpectedly. Fourth, ensure ARRaycastManager and ARPlaneManager are children of the same AR Session Origin so coordinates align. A common misconception is blaming the placement code when the real issue is environmental; always test in multiple lighting and texture conditions. Example fix: create a visible plane prefab, test in a well‑lit room with textured surfaces, and verify managers are on AR Session Origin. Key takeaway: isolate whether the problem is visualization, tracking quality, or hierarchy/setup, then apply the matching remedy.

content.html:
Troubleshooting

Why planes aren't visible

  • Plane Prefab slot is empty or prefab lacks AR Plane component.
  • Material is opaque and blocking the camera feed.
  • Poor lighting or textureless surfaces prevent detection.
Fix
Assign a translucent prefab with AR Plane component, test in textured, well-lit areas, and confirm AR managers are on the AR Session Origin.
Why objects drift
Drift often signals tracking issues or a misconfigured origin. Confirm the AR Camera is a child of AR Session Origin and that the origin hasn't been transformed after tracking starts. Also test on-device movement patterns to ensure consistent tracking quality.
Check list
Plane Prefab, AR managers placement, lighting, and device motion when testing.
Testing tip
Walk slowly and vary viewpoints to help the system build a more complete map during testing.
Key Takeaway

Start with prefab and hierarchy checks, then validate environment and device motion before debugging placement code.

Hands-on Activity

Visualize planes and place a cube

  1. Select AR Session Origin and add AR Plane Manager and ARRaycastManager components.
  2. Create a Quad named ARPlaneVisualizer and a material set to Fade/Transparent. Tint it light blue and set alpha to ~40%.

  5. Create or paste the ARPlacementManager script into your project and attach it to AR Session Origin. Assign ARCubePrefab to objectToPlace.
  6. Build to a device, scan a textured, well-lit area, and tap a detected plane to place your cube.
Checks and tips
  • If no planes appear, confirm the Plane Prefab is assigned and has AR Plane component.
  • Test in varied lighting and textured areas to improve detection reliability.
  • Adjust material alpha to balance visibility and realism for the user.
Reflection
After placing the cube, scan more of the scene. Watch plane polygons change and think about whether you need to reanchor objects after merges or updates.
Key Takeaway

Follow the exact setup steps and test on a real device. Environment quality has more impact than code in many plane detection issues.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how an AR system turns raw camera frames and sensor data into a usable map of the world by detecting flat surfaces. Plane detection is the foundation for believable AR: it tells your app where floors, tabletops, and walls are so virtual content can rest convincingly. We'll walk through how Unity's AR Foundation exposes that information through the AR Plane Manager and AR Plane objects, how to visualize planes with a semi‑transparent prefab, and how a raycast from a user tap yields the exact pose where an object can be spawned. You'll also learn the role of AR Session and AR Session Origin in keeping coordinates consistent across the real world and Unity's scene. Finally, we'll cover practical troubleshooting so you know why planes may not appear or why content might drift. By the end, you will be able to add plane visualization, allow simple tap placement, and interpret common tracking issues when testing on a device.

We begin by setting clear, demonstrable objectives so you know what to practice. First, you'll explain how AR platforms detect and track planes: what a plane trackable is, why poses and boundary polygons matter, and how continuous scanning refines those surfaces. Second, you'll be able to use Unity's AR Foundation components to visualize planes in a scene — create a semi‑transparent prefab, assign it to the AR Plane Manager, and understand how the manager instantiates AR Plane GameObjects. Third, you'll implement logic to interact with detected planes using raycasts so taps on the screen produce precise world poses and objects appear where the user expects. Fourth, you'll describe the AR Session and AR Session Origin roles so you can diagnose placement and scaling issues. Each objective links a practical task to why it matters in real apps and sets you up for the hands‑on activity that follows.

This second objectives slide ties each learning goal to a concrete practice and a quick mnemonic to remember the steps. First, when you explain plane detection, practice by observing how plane polygons expand or merge as you move around a scene; that shows the system refining its map. Second, when you visualize planes, create a translucent quad prefab and confirm it shows the real world beneath—this prevents confusion about missing planes. Third, when implementing tap placement, test touches on the plane boundary and center; using TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon prevents placement outside the detected area. Fourth, for session and origin, move the device and watch how the AR Camera and your virtual content stay aligned; if things drift, you'll know where to check. These practice actions make each objective testable and help you recognize common mistakes quickly.

Plane detection is the process where the AR platform analyzes camera images and device motion to identify flat, roughly planar surfaces in the environment. A detected plane is represented as a trackable with a pose — a position and rotation in 3D space — and a boundary polygon that outlines the shape and size of the area recognized so far. This gives your app three essential pieces of information: where to place objects, how to orient them to match the surface, and the usable area so you avoid placing content beyond the detected region. For example, if a table is detected, the AR system reports the table's center pose and a polygon that follows its visible edges; you can then place a model so it sits flush with the table top. A common misconception is to expect a perfectly complete polygon immediately. In reality, plane polygons refine over time as the system receives more visual data: they can grow, shrink, and merge. That means your placement logic should tolerate updates — avoid relying on a single momentary polygon size. Key takeaway: treat detected planes as evolving anchors that provide pose and boundary information you can use for grounded placement, but always handle updates and merges gracefully.

Unity's AR Foundation provides the AR Plane Manager to bridge the underlying AR SDK's plane detections into your scene. When you add an AR Plane Manager to the AR Session Origin, it listens for plane trackable events and can instantiate a prefab to represent each detected plane. That prefab should include a Mesh Renderer/Mesh Filter or a simple Quad and an AR Plane component so the manager recognizes it as a visual representation. The AR Plane Manager can be configured to detect horizontal, vertical, or both plane types; choose the types your experience requires to reduce noise. As the AR system updates planes, the AR Plane Manager updates the corresponding GameObjects so the pose and mesh reflect the refined polygon. A common misunderstanding is thinking the manager itself performs detection; instead, it coordinates detections from ARCore/ARKit and manages Unity GameObjects. Practical example: create a semi‑transparent quad prefab named ARPlaneVisualizer, assign a translucent material, add the AR Plane component, and drag that prefab into the Plane Prefab slot on the AR Plane Manager. This ensures visible feedback during testing and helps users and developers see what the runtime perceives as usable surface. Close by asking: how will you tune plane types and materials to balance visibility and real‑world readability?

Making a clear plane visual is a small authoring step that pays off during testing and user interaction. The process begins in Unity's Project window: create a Quad or simple mesh and name it 'ARPlaneVisualizer'. Next, create a material and choose a translucent rendering mode such as Fade or Transparent; pick a light, distinctive tint so planes are visible without obscuring the camera feed. Assign that material to the quad so the real world remains visible beneath the visual. Add the AR Plane component to the visual so Unity treats the prefab properly when instantiated by AR Plane Manager. Finally, convert the GameObject into a prefab by dragging it into Assets and then delete the scene instance to keep the hierarchy clean. A common mistake is using an opaque material — doing so hides real-world cues and confuses testing. Practical example: use a pale blue with alpha around 40% so the boundary is easy to see while still revealing floor or tabletop texture. When done, assign this prefab to the Plane Prefab slot on the AR Plane Manager attached to your AR Session Origin. Practice this sequence to make plane detection immediately visible on device builds.

This lesson walks through the core placement logic that turns a screen touch into a world pose and a spawned object. The ARRaycastManager handles raycasts against trackables such as detected planes. In the provided script, the script gets the ARRaycastManager reference in Awake, then in Update checks for touches. When a touch begins, the code calls Raycast with TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon so hits are restricted to the interior of detected plane polygons. If a hit exists, it uses the first hit's pose to instantiate the prefab at that position with the plane's rotation. A concrete example: tapping the tabletop sends a ray through the camera frustum that intersects the plane polygon where the table was detected; the script instantiates the cube prefab at that pose so it visually rests on the table. A common misconception is assuming raycasts return every frame without touches; raycasts should be targeted on user input to avoid unnecessary instantiation. Also, because planes update, instantiated objects reference the pose at spawn time — consider parenting objects or reanchoring them if you need them to follow a plane's geometry later. This script is intentionally small so you can extend it to check for multiple hits, add placement indicators, or constrain placement by plane size.

Two foundational GameObjects control the AR runtime in Unity: AR Session and AR Session Origin. AR Session manages the lifecycle — starting, pausing, and stopping tracking — and acts as the bridge to the platform's tracking engine. AR Session Origin is the coordinate translation layer: it maps the real‑world tracking coordinate system provided by ARKit or ARCore into Unity's world space so your virtual content appears in the correct physical location. The AR Camera is commonly a child of AR Session Origin; when the device moves, the AR Camera's transform changes to keep the background and overlays aligned. A common pitfall is adding AR Plane Manager or ARRaycastManager to a GameObject outside AR Session Origin; both should be on AR Session Origin or a child so their trackable coordinates match the origin's coordinate space. For example, if you spawn content under AR Session Origin, and then later accidentally move the origin, all your virtual content will shift relative to the camera. Key practical check: when things drift or placement seems offset, inspect whether AR Session Origin has been scaled, rotated, or otherwise modified. The main takeaway is that AR Session handles tracking lifecycle while AR Session Origin defines where and how trackables map into your Unity scene.

Detected planes have a lifecycle: they are created when enough features are found, updated as new observations expand or refine their boundary, merged when overlapping detections represent the same surface, and sometimes removed when tracking loses confidence. Understanding this lifecycle helps you build robust placement and UI behaviors. For example, when two small plane polygons merge into one larger polygon, an object you previously anchored to the first plane still has its original pose; the AR Plane Manager will update mesh geometry but not necessarily reparent or reposition your object — your code should decide if it needs to re-anchor or keep the original pose. A concrete example: you detect two adjacent patches on a long table; as you walk, the SDK merges them into a single plane. If your placement logic expects a fixed polygon size, placements near the seam could be rejected earlier and accepted later. A common mistake is assuming plane boundaries are permanent. Instead, design UI affordances that indicate scanning is ongoing and either delay final placement until a plane stabilizes or allow users to move objects after placement. The key insight is planning for dynamic updates — handle creates, updates, merges, and removals gracefully so content remains believable and stable.

ARRaycastManager supports different TrackableType flags that control what surfaces raycasts can hit. TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon confines hits to the interior of a detected plane's boundary — a good default for placing objects strictly on a known surface. If you need hits on estimated infinite planes or approximate ground alignment, other flags or custom logic may be appropriate. For example, PlaneWithinPolygon prevents placement on the invisible extension of a table beyond the detected area, which is often what you want to avoid floating objects or unexpected overlaps. A contrasting choice is using PlaneEstimated or FeaturePoint hits when you want looser placement semantics: feature points let you place on textured surfaces that were not yet consolidated into a plane, but they are less stable. A common mistake is mixing trackable types without understanding stability tradeoffs; using feature points can yield placements that look correct momentarily but drift as tracking refines. Concrete example: for a furniture placement app, use PlaneWithinPolygon for reliable anchored placement on tabletops and floors. For an exploratory game that places ephemeral items in rough locations, feature or estimated hits may be acceptable. The core decision is balancing placement stability against availability when surfaces are difficult to detect.

When plane visuals don't appear or placed objects drift, a few recurring causes explain most situations. First, if plane visuals are missing, check whether the Plane Prefab slot on AR Plane Manager is empty or the assigned prefab lacks an AR Plane component. Without that prefab, the manager has nothing to instantiate visually even though detection may be happening. Second, poor tracking due to textureless surfaces, low light, or reflective materials reduces feature points and delays plane creation. A practical diagnostic is to move the device slowly across textured regions; if detection improves, tracking conditions were the culprit. Third, if objects drift, confirm AR Session Origin and AR Camera are set up correctly and not being transformed after tracking begins. Also check that the AR Session hasn't been restarted unexpectedly. Fourth, ensure ARRaycastManager and ARPlaneManager are children of the same AR Session Origin so coordinates align. A common misconception is blaming the placement code when the real issue is environmental; always test in multiple lighting and texture conditions. Example fix: create a visible plane prefab, test in a well‑lit room with textured surfaces, and verify managers are on AR Session Origin. Key takeaway: isolate whether the problem is visualization, tracking quality, or hierarchy/setup, then apply the matching remedy.
